rows.content_mid: f Time and Tail Current:** When the gate voltage is removed (or pulled negative, typically -8V to -15V), the IGBT turns off. However, unlike a MOSFET, an IGBT experiences a phenomenon called **tail current**. Because of its BJT-like structure, minority carriers take a brief moment to sweep out of the base region. This causes the current to trail off slowly rather than dropping instantly. This tail current generates heat (switching losses). If the switching frequency is set too high in the VFD parameters, the IGBT spends too much time in this lossy state and will overheat.
### Gate Driver Circuits

The microprocessor in a VFD operates at 3.3V or 5V. An IGBT requires +15V to turn on fully and often a negative voltage (e.g., -8V) to turn off cleanly and prevent false triggering from electrical noise (dv/dt transients).

The **Gate Driver** is the intermediary circuit. It takes the low-voltage logic signal and amplifies it to drive the IGBT gate. Crucially, gate drivers provide **galvanic isolation** (usually via optocouplers or pulse transformers) to protect the sensitive control board from the lethal voltages on the DC bus.
### IGBT Module Packages: The 6-Pack
While you can buy discrete, single IGBTs (looking like large transistors), industrial VFDs almost exclusively use **IGBT Modules**.

A standard 3-phase AC motor requires six switches to create the three AC phases (two switches per phase: one pulling up to the positive DC bus, one pulling down to the negative DC bus). Manufacturers package all six IGBTs, along with their antiparallel freewheeling diodes, into a single block known as a **6-pack module**.
When one IGBT in a 6-pack blows, you replace the entire module.
### Thermal Management

IGBTs generate heat—lots of it. A 100A IGBT module might dissipate several hundred watts. If this heat isn't removed, the silicon will exceed its maximum junction temperature (usually 150°C to 175°C) and fail catastrophically.
- **Heatsink:** The module is bolted to a massive aluminum heatsink.

- **Thermal Paste:** Microscopic imperfections in the metal surfaces trap air, which is a terrible conductor of heat. Thermal grease (or a thermal pad) fills these gaps. **Too much paste is just as bad as too little.** It should be a paper-thin, translucent layer.
- **Cooling Fans:** VFDs rely on high-CFM fans to push air across the heatsink fins.

> **Technician Tip:** 90% of VFD overheating faults are caused by clogged heatsink fins or dead cooling fans. Before you start meggering motors or replacing drives, take an air hose to the heatsink and verify the fans are actually spinning at full speed.
## Practical Reference Data
### Table 1: IGBT vs. MOSFET vs. BJT Comparison
| Characteristic | MOSFET | BJT | IGBT |
| **Control Method** | Voltage (Gate) | Current (Base) | Voltage (Gate) |
| **Switching Speed** | Very Fast (>100 kHz) | Slow (<10 kHz) | Medium (2 kHz - 50 kHz) |
| **High Voltage/Current Handling** | Poor/Moderate |
